formativeChecks.question: A player is sweating after a warm-up. What can you reasonably conclude?
choices: They must be afraid of losing.
Sweating alone does not establish anxiety; more context is needed.
Their performance will now get worse.
formativeChecks.feedback: A bodily signal can have several causes. Ask about the situation and the athlete’s experience before interpreting it.

formativeChecks.question: An athlete says, “My heart is beating faster and I feel alert. I am not worried.” Which term best describes the information given?
choices: Arousal
Cognitive anxiety
Trait anxiety
formativeChecks.feedback: Arousal describes activation. The athlete has specifically said they are not worried. A fast heartbeat alone does not establish cognitive or trait anxiety.

formativeChecks.question: An athlete says, “I feel nervous: my shoulders are tight and I have butterflies.” Which anxiety component is being described?
choices: Cognitive state anxiety
Somatic state anxiety
A long-term personality disposition
formativeChecks.feedback: The description concerns perceived bodily sensations in this moment: the somatic component of state anxiety.

formativeChecks.question: Which statement belongs to Stage 2 rather than Stage 1?
choices: The athlete is taking a penalty kick.
The athlete sees the kick as a chance to use a practised skill.
The athlete kicks the ball wide.
formativeChecks.feedback: Stage 2 is the perception or appraisal of the demand. Taking the kick is the demand; the result belongs to the behavioural consequences.

formativeChecks.question: A learner says, “Drive Theory means getting more excited will fix my technique.” What is missing?
choices: More arousal guarantees that every habit improves.
A stronger dominant response can still be an incorrect response.
Practice becomes unnecessary once arousal is high.
formativeChecks.feedback: The important question is which response is strongest. Extra activation does not replace skill practice or guarantee the correct technique.

formativeChecks.question: Two athletes describe different levels of state anxiety during their best performances. Which model most directly emphasizes those different personal ranges?
choices: Drive Theory
The Inverted-U Hypothesis
IZOF
formativeChecks.feedback: IZOF emphasizes an individual best-performance range. The Inverted-U explains a rise-and-fall pattern; its drawing is not a universal target number. Drive Theory asks about the strength of the dominant response.

formativeChecks.question: A swimmer is nervous before a difficult race. Which reframe links the demand to a real resource?
choices: I cannot lose if I think positively.
Good athletes never feel nervous.
This race is demanding. I can use my practised start and first-race cue.
formativeChecks.feedback: A believable reframe accepts the challenge and names a resource or action. It does not promise a result or require all nerves to disappear.

formativeChecks.question: Which combination is central to the Catastrophe model?
choices: High cognitive anxiety together with high physiological arousal
Low activation with no worry
Any increase in heart rate
formativeChecks.feedback: The model combines high cognitive anxiety with high physiological arousal. It predicts the possibility of a sharp drop, not merely a small decline as activation rises.

formativeChecks.question: A student is nervous because the assessment instructions are unclear. What is the most direct first response?
choices: Assume they have high trait anxiety.
Tell them to use more positive thinking and ignore the instructions.
Clarify the task and success criteria with the teacher.
formativeChecks.feedback: The stated source is uncertainty about the task. Clarifying it addresses the source. A regulation tool may still be useful, but it cannot supply missing instructions.

formativeChecks.question: A student says, “I am not sure what the coach will evaluate at the tryout.” Which situational source is most directly described?
choices: Uncertainty
Trait anxiety
Social physique anxiety
formativeChecks.feedback: The statement concerns unclear evaluation. That is uncertainty in the situation, rather than evidence of a stable disposition or worry about body evaluation.

formativeChecks.question: Which explanation best describes useful attention?
choices: Always notice as many things as possible.
Always use the narrowest focus possible.
Select the information needed for the current task, and widen or narrow when the task changes.
formativeChecks.feedback: Attention must fit the task. A precise aiming task and a changing team play can need different amounts of information.

formativeChecks.question: A player watches one opponent so closely that they miss a teammate signalling for a pass. What is the best explanation from this lesson?
choices: Every form of narrow attention improves performance.
Attention has narrowed enough to hide a relevant cue.
The player must have no arousal.
formativeChecks.feedback: The important feature is the missed relevant information. Narrowing is not automatically a problem; it becomes a problem when it prevents the athlete from detecting what the task requires.

formativeChecks.question: An athlete feels flat, has low energy and is easily distracted. Which first move best matches the regulation toolkit?
choices: Keep lowering activation with more relaxation.
Use appropriate movement or rhythm to raise activation.
Focus only on winning the event.
formativeChecks.feedback: The described problem is under-arousal. The toolkit matches low activation with movement, rhythm, music or imagery rather than automatically choosing relaxation.

formativeChecks.question: A player uses the planned routine and misses the shot. What is the most useful review?
choices: The routine definitely failed because the shot missed.
Record the routine and result separately; review the pattern across more attempts.
The result does not matter, so no review is needed.
formativeChecks.feedback: A single result does not establish cause. Check the planned action, the quality of the attempt and the outcome, then look for a pattern.

formativeChecks.question: Which statement is a process goal?
choices: Win the match.
Record a personal-best time.
Complete my preparation routine before each attempt.
formativeChecks.feedback: A process goal specifies an action. Winning is an outcome; a personal-best time is a performance standard.

assets.alt: The same penalty shot can be seen as a threat to the player’s worth or as a difficult task supported by a practised routine. Neither interpretation guarantees the result.
assets.caption: ONE SITUATION, DIFFERENT MEANINGS. The task is unchanged. The example compares possible interpretations—not “strong” and “weak” kinds of athlete.

assets.alt: A chapter map linking arousal, anxiety, stress, attention, regulation tools and perceived control with the ideal performance state.
assets.caption: YOUR LEARNING MAP. You will learn each part before bringing the parts together in your Regulation Engine.

assets.alt: Possible pressure signals include worried thoughts, muscle tension, sweaty or shaky hands, a faster heartbeat, quicker breathing and an unsettled stomach. The athlete is fictional; these signs have more than one possible cause.
assets.caption: NOTICE THE PATTERN. These are possible signals, not a checklist that proves anxiety. Read the athlete’s own account and consider the situation.

assets.alt: Arousal ranges from low activation through an ideal performance zone to high activation.
assets.caption: READ THE CONTINUUM. The middle zone is an introductory model. Later, IZOF explains why athletes do not all have the same best-performance range.

assets.alt: The stress loop moves from environmental demand to perception of the demand, to stress response, to behavioural consequences and back around.
assets.caption: THE PIVOT POINT. Appraisal is the athlete’s interpretation of the demand, not the demand itself.

assets.alt: Four schematic models: Drive Theory strengthens the dominant response; the Inverted-U predicts a rise and fall; IZOF shows different personal state-anxiety ranges; Catastrophe allows a sharp drop when cognitive anxiety and physiological arousal are high.
assets.caption: COMPARE THE QUESTION EACH MODEL ASKS. These are teaching diagrams, not a graph of your own body or performance. The rising Drive line illustrates the well-practised-response case.

assets.alt: Three views of a player’s attention: too broad at low arousal, selectively focused at a useful level, and too narrow at high arousal.
assets.caption: FOLLOW THE INFORMATION. Selective attention is useful when it keeps relevant information available. Tunnel vision is a problem when important cues disappear.

assets.alt: The source toolkit groups breathing, activation and relaxation, cue words and SMART goals around state regulation.
assets.caption: YOUR REGULATION TOOLKIT. Each tool serves a different purpose. Cue words and SMART goals are developed in the next topic.

assets.alt: A goal ladder compares lower-control outcome goals, partly controllable performance goals and higher-control process goals.
assets.caption: MOVE TOWARD ACTION. Compare outcome, performance and process goals according to how directly the athlete can control them.
